title: Catalog: m/n = 1/x + 1/y (two unit fractions; Stewart 1964 criterion)
connection: m/n = 1/x + 1/y (two unit fractions; Stewart 1964 criterion) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(d(n)) — tiny. Obstruction: local+multiplicative: needs coprime divisors a,b of n with m | a+b. Status: fully characterised; for fixed m almost all n work, asymptotic for exceptions (Elsholtz 1998, Huang–Vaughan 2011); 4/p never works for p ≡ 1 mod 4. Mechanism: divisor criterion: exceptions = n whose prime factors lie in a subgroup of (ℤ/m)^× avoiding −1.
why: The k = 2 analogue of ES is completely understood: failure ⟺ prime factors in a subgroup avoiding −1. ES's E1/E2 events are this criterion applied to p-tied auxiliary integers.
first_step: Recast ES as: ∃ auxiliary integer N(p, params) whose prime factors are NOT confined to a subgroup avoiding −1 mod 4C; list which subgroups are forced at squares (T1).

title: Catalog: Schinzel: m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n > N_m (fixed m ≥ 4)
connection: Schinzel: m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n > N_m (fixed m ≥ 4) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ (log p)³/m at primes (Pomerance–Weingartner heuristic). Obstruction: none local for large n. Status: open for every m ≥ 4; Pomerance–Weingartner: N_m ≥ exp(m^{1/3−ε}) (most primes near exp(m^{1/3−ε}) fail). Mechanism: Brun–Titchmarsh upper bound on Type I/II solvable primes when count (log p)³/m ≪ 1; Poisson heuristic predicts transition to 'always' at p ≈ exp(m^{1/2+o(1)}).
why: Gives a one-parameter family crossing the dividing line: m/p moves from 'mostly false' to 'always true' as p grows; ES is m = 4 at the 'always' end. Very direct calibration.
first_step: Compute for m = 8..40 the largest exceptional prime up to 10^9 and fit log N_m vs log m (prediction exponent 1/2); does m = 4's empirical margin match?
alt_first_steps: [signature-0049] Check the PW lower-bound construction for exceptions and whether its mechanism (covering by many small primes) can be run at m = 4.
refs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.16817 (Pomerance–Weingartner, Exceptions to the Erdős–Straus–Schinzel conjecture)

connection: Erdős–Graham colouring conjecture (monochromatic Σ1/x = 1) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (Croot 2003). Mechanism: Fourier/smooth numbers.
why: Density/colouring versions of unit-fraction problems are provable (abundance); control.

title: Catalog: Bloom: positive-density sets contain S with Σ_{n∈S} 1/n = 1
connection: Bloom: positive-density sets contain S with Σ_{n∈S} 1/n = 1 ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: power. Obstruction: none. Status: proved (Bloom 2021). Mechanism: Fourier analysis on unit fractions.

title: Catalog: Zaremba: every q has a/q with partial quotients ≤ 5
connection: Zaremba: every q has a/q with partial quotients ≤ 5 ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ q^{2δ_5 − 1} (power). Obstruction: none. Status: claimed proved (Zhang 2605.02518v2, unrefereed); Bourgain–Kontorovich almost all (A = 50). Mechanism: thin-orbit expansion in SL₂(ℤ/q); alphabet size tunes the count.
why: ES₅ is a CF-length-3 question; Zaremba's count is a tunable power, ES's is fixed log².

title: Catalog: Hensley's conjecture (δ_A > 1/2 ⇒ almost all q)
connection: Hensley's conjecture (δ_A > 1/2 ⇒ almost all q) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: q^{2δ_A − 1}. Obstruction: congruence obstruction for A = {2,4,6,8,10}. Status: false as stated (Bourgain–Kontorovich); corrected forms open. Mechanism: local obstruction mod small moduli.
why: Count crossing 1 at δ_A = 1/2 is the exact dividing line for power-count orbits; ES sits at count log², i.e. 'δ = 1/2 + logarithmic'.
first_step: Find an alphabet A with δ_A = 1/2 (critical) and look at what is known: is ES₅ a 'critical-exponent' thin orbit problem?

title: Rickards–Stange reciprocity obstruction as the model of T1
connection: RS prove semigroup orbits in SL₂(ℤ) can miss squares through a reciprocity obstruction (Jacobi symbols on the orbit), with finitely many sporadic exceptions in the 'fat' case. QUESTION_R casts ES as such a thin orbit with T1 as the reciprocity obstruction.
why: It is the nearest proved local-global-with-reciprocity theorem. The native next step is to place ES₅/U(n) inside an RS-type semigroup.
first_step: Already pursued (QUESTION_R). Here: check whether U(n)'s six sporadics fit an RS 'sporadic set' pattern (e.g. explained by a finite-index sub-orbit).
alt_first_steps: [tools-0305] Factor the sporadic n (105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, …) and look for a common local feature (all divisible by 3? all ≡ 1 mod 8?).

connection: Congruent numbers: primes p ≡ 5,7 mod 8 are congruent ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: rank-1 Heegner point: 1 generator. Obstruction: root number. Status: proved for every such prime (Heegner, Monsky; Tian extends to many n). Mechanism: Heegner points / modular parametrisation.

unverified: Monsky, Mock Heegner points and congruent numbers (1990s)

title: Catalog: Congruent numbers n ≡ 5,6,7 mod 8 (all) — Smith distribution
connection: Congruent numbers n ≡ 5,6,7 mod 8 (all) — Smith distribution ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: rank parity. Obstruction: root number forces odd rank. Status: 100% of n ≡ 5,6,7 mod 8 (Smith); all such n conditional on BSD. Mechanism: Selmer group distribution (Smith's method) + parity.
why: 'Parity forces existence' is a powerful pointwise mechanism (rank odd ⇒ point exists, given finiteness of Sha). ES has no parity-forced object known.
first_step: Look for an elliptic curve or Selmer-type group attached to p whose rank parity is forced by p ≡ 1 mod 4 and which maps to ES solutions.

first_step: Check the exact hypotheses of Dasgupta–Voight 'Sylvester's problem and mock Heegner points'.

title: Dividing-line reading of the computation: ES is a 'random covering' with log³ intensity, Crocker's problem a 'random covering' with log intensity
connection: In the residue model, ES's hit intensity grows like (log X)³ (families up to X), so failures become rarer than any power of X; p + 2^a + 2^b has intensity ≈ log n, giving failure probability ≈ n^{−c}, compatible with infinitely many structured failures.

title: Result: ES certificate families are strongly positively correlated (residue model), yet coverage still decays like exp(−c log³ X)

title: Result: ES difficulty tracks the least quadratic non-residue n(p) ('pseudosquare-ness')

why: Primes that look like squares to many small quadratic characters are harder — T1 at actual squares is the limit of this trend. A proof route: 'ES-hardness ≤ function of quadratic-character pattern', with genuine non-squares eventually escaping. EVIDENCE.
first_step: Replace n(p) by the number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = +1 and by the full character vector; fit s(p) with a regression or tree; look at the residual for the 2814 record.
